CT0: Cybersecurity Transformer

Víctor Mayoral-Vilches Affiliation: Alias Robotics, Vitoria-Gasteiz, Álava, Spain
Abstract

General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and alias3-micro, its first incarnation: a compact (∼\sim4 B-parameter) model built on the open Qwen3.5-4B base, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: alias3-micro solves 21.1%21.1\% of cybench-subtask against 7.6%7.6\% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: alias3-micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5%96.5\% accuracy in 4747 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5%76.5\% in 254254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.9660.966 in 88 ms, and, generating only for the facts it is unsure about, extracts vulnerability facts more accurately than either mode alone at a fifth of the generative cost. All of it is built in about 314314 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours and served from one workstation GPU, with no policy layer between operator and target. Across eighteen benchmarks and use cases run with one checkpoint and head, we report where the design helps, where it does not, and what it still lacks.

1  Introduction

The dominant recipe for Cybersecurity AI consists of post-training a large general-purpose model with security-related RL environments, a model that was never architected for the domain [aliasrobotics2025cai, mayoralvilchescybersuper2026] adapting its weights to security use cases. Four costs follow. Price and latency: frontier inference is expensive and slow relative to the tight loops of offensive-security work. Control: closed weights cannot be inspected, fine-tuned to a house methodology, run air-gapped on a client’s premises, or audited. Refusal: alignment layers calibrated for consumer products routinely decline legitimate, authorised defensive work; we have observed frontier models halt mid-engagement on authorised forensic targets, citing usage policy. Privacy: every prompt to a hosted model carries the client’s most sensitive material, such as credentials, configurations, telemetry and unpatched vulnerabilities, off the premises and into a third party’s logs and retention policies, which many engagements, regulated sectors and non-disclosure terms do not permit; a specialist that runs locally keeps that material where the contract says it must stay.

We ask the opposite question: how small can a transformer be while remaining a genuinely useful cybersecurity specialist? A specialist that runs on one workstation GPU, can be further fine-tuned to a methodology, and sits with no policy layer between operator and target changes both the economics and the control surface of the field.

We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture depicted in figure 2, and alias3-micro, its first incarnation: a ∼\sim4 B-parameter model post-trained from an open base into a dual-mode agent. CT0 makes two commitments. (i) One backbone, two inference regimes. Following dual-process accounts of cognition [kahneman2011thinking], a fast System-1 mode answers typed decisions (classify, score, triage) during prefill through a bilinear pointer head adapted from the Jev/System One lineage [vinyals2015pointer, typesafe2026systemone], decoding zero tokens; the usual System-2 agentic decode loop runs from the same weight set; an external controller routes between them. (ii) Specialisation by on-policy distillation. The backbone is distilled on-policy [agarwal2024onpolicy] from a larger open teacher over its own rollouts on the CAI dataset [aliasrobotics2025cai], in two chained phases.

Table 1 summarises the evidence, and its strongest rows concern how computation is used. System 1 detects refusals at 96.5%96.5\% accuracy in 4747 ms where generative self-judging reaches 76.5%76.5\% in 254254 ms and misses half of them; it screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise (IOC); and preserving confident typed facts while repairing uncertain ones raises exact match on synthetic findings to 48.3%48.3\% from 43.4%43.4\% (S1) and 38.0%38.0\% (S2) at a fifth of the generative cost. Specialisation lifts the agentic path as well: under the fixed local budget of Section  the specialist solves 36/17136/171 (21.1%21.1\%) of cybench-subtask, 2.8×2.8\times its open base (7.6%7.6\%) and above Gemma-4 E4B (12.7%12.7\%), the ternary-weight Bonsai 2 27B (8.2%8.2\%) and the 78 B mixture-of-experts Kolibri-1 (5.3%5.3\%); the alias series then scales to 40.940.9 and 56.1%56.1\%. Where a cheap first stage drops the evidence the generator needs, composition loses, and Section  says where; Section  gathers everything the evidence does not support.
